landing.faq.heading: Questions, answered.
landing.faq.manifestoLink: Why tasks and issues stop you moving toward goals.
landing.faq.q1.answer: Because almost no one actually moves more than 2 at a time. The cap isn't restrictive — it's protective. If you can't pick 3, you'll fail at all of them.
landing.faq.q1.question: Why only 3 goals?
landing.faq.q2.answer: ActOS isn't built for that load. Tasks unrelated to your 2-3 goals don't belong here. If you're juggling 200 items, the real question is why you took them all on.
landing.faq.q2.question: What if I have 200 things to do?
landing.faq.q3.answer: No. Todo apps optimize for capturing things to do. ActOS optimizes for moving toward things you decided matter. Different problem, different design.
landing.faq.q3.question: Is this just another todo app?
landing.faq.q4.answer: Yes. The web app works on phones today. Native iOS and Android apps come post-launch.
landing.faq.q4.question: Does it work on mobile?
landing.faq.q5.answer: It is — to start. The Free tier is genuinely useful, not a limited demo. All-In is $12/mo for people ready to commit. We charge because focus is worth paying for, and we want to build sustainably without ads or VC pressure.
landing.faq.q5.question: Why isn't it free forever?
landing.hero.subline: The OS for getting things done.

manifesto.closing.line1: If you want to try it,
manifesto.closing.line2: . Free is real and the trial doesn't expire.
manifesto.closing.line3: If you don't, I hope at least the framing was useful. The goal isn't to convert you to a product. The goal is to convert you to a way of working.
manifesto.closing.line4: Tasks won't get you there. Action will.
manifesto.deck: Why I built ActOS after eight years of failing at productivity tools.
manifesto.h2_1: Tasks are a trap dressed as a solution
manifesto.h2_4: The hardest part is the cap
manifesto.h2_5: What I'd ask you to try
manifesto.li1: Every action belongs to a project. Every project belongs to a goal. Nothing exists outside that hierarchy. There's no inbox. No "miscellaneous." If something doesn't tie to a goal, it doesn't enter the system.
manifesto.li2: You can have **at most 3 active goals**. Not as a guideline — as a hard cap the product enforces. The "+ New goal" button literally stops working if you try to add a fourth.
manifesto.li3: Each day, the product asks one question: *what single thing makes today a win?* That's the Main Task. Everything else is bonus.
manifesto.li4: Every action carries an Impact score (1-10) and a time estimate. The product surfaces high-impact work, so you don't spend Tuesday on something that doesn't matter.
manifesto.p1: For eight years, I tried every productivity tool that promised to make me focused. Todoist. Things. Notion. TickTick. Trello. Sunsama. Linear. Asana. Four custom Notion templates I built myself between failed jobs.
manifesto.p10: The system was crude — a text file, a sticky note, no automation, no integrations. But the *shape* of it was right. It separated "things I'm doing" from "things that move me forward." It made the second category small enough to actually act on.
manifesto.p11: That's the shape ActOS gives form to.
manifesto.p12: It looks like one, on the surface. You'll see actions with checkboxes, a Today view, a Main Task for the day. The components are familiar.
manifesto.p13: But underneath, the structure is different:
manifesto.p15: ActOS refuses to capture your busywork. It refuses to let you "track" 200 things. It refuses to give you the dopamine hit of checking off 47 items when none of them moved a goal.
manifesto.p16: The 3-goal limit is the most controversial decision in the product, and it's also the one I'm least willing to negotiate on.
manifesto.p17: Almost everyone who's serious about something has more than 3 things they're "working on." Almost no one is actually making meaningful progress on more than 2.
manifesto.p18: If you can't pick 3, the tool can't help you. It's not the tool's job to give you permission to be unfocused. It's the tool's job to reflect the reality that focus is the entire game.
manifesto.p19: I know this filters out a lot of potential customers. That's intentional. ActOS isn't for everyone — it's for people who've already decided that they want to do fewer things, more seriously.
manifesto.p2: I'd set up the new system on a Sunday evening — clean databases, color-coded tags, perfect filters. By Wednesday I'd be back to the same problem: I was completing 30 things a week and the projects I actually cared about hadn't moved.
manifesto.p20: Stop scheduling tasks for a week. Pick 2 goals you actually care about. Each morning, decide the one thing that makes today a win for those goals. Do that thing.
manifesto.p21: You can use ActOS. You can use a sticky note. The tool isn't what matters — the *shape* matters.
manifesto.p22: If a sticky note works for you, keep using it. I built ActOS because I wanted that shape with a little more structure, a little more memory, a little more ability to look back at where the weeks went. That's all the product is. It's the smallest version of "the system I actually use" that I could ship.
manifesto.p3: The tool wasn't the problem. The category was.
manifesto.p4: A task is anything that takes effort. "Reply to Mark." "Schedule dentist." "Buy paper towels." All tasks. None of them move you toward who you want to become. But because they live in the same list as the things that *do* matter — your training plan, your draft, your business — the trivial and the meaningful compete for the same checkbox.
manifesto.p5: The trivial always wins. It's easier. It generates a dopamine hit faster. By Friday you've done 47 things and made zero progress on the one thing this week was supposed to be about.
manifesto.p6: Tasks expand to fill the day. Goals get squeezed out.
manifesto.p7: This isn't a tooling problem. It's a category error. The premise of task management is "if I capture everything, I'll feel in control." But the cost of "everything" is that nothing's important. A list of 200 items isn't a plan. It's a noise floor.
manifesto.p8: I stopped using task apps for goals. I kept a separate file — just one — with 2-3 things I cared about that quarter. Every morning I asked one question: *what single thing today makes this week a win?* I'd write it down. Then I'd do that thing, even if the rest of my day was a mess of meetings and "tasks."
manifesto.p9: Within three months I'd shipped more on those 2-3 goals than I had in the previous two years.
manifesto.pullquote: Tasks gave me 47 checkmarks a week. Action moves toward 2-3 goals. That's the difference.
manifesto.title: Tasks won't get you there.

pricing.faq.heading: Common questions.
pricing.faq.q1.answer: Yes. Upgrade or downgrade any time from Settings → Subscription. Annual subscribers can switch to monthly at renewal.
pricing.faq.q1.question: Can I change plans later?
pricing.faq.q2.answer: You stay on All-In until the end of the billing period you already paid for. After that, the account drops to Free — your data stays intact. Active entities (goals, projects, actions) are never locked; only history older than 90 days becomes view-only.
pricing.faq.q2.question: What happens when I cancel?
pricing.faq.q3.answer: For new subscribers, possibly — we may raise prices as we add features. But once you subscribe, your price is locked. Existing subscribers never see a hike as long as the subscription stays active.
pricing.faq.q3.question: Will the price go up?
pricing.faq.q4.answer: Free is the trial. It's a full version of the product with no time limit — not a teaser. If 90 days of history and 2 goals isn't enough, that's the signal you're ready for All-In.
pricing.faq.q4.question: Why isn't there a free trial of All-In?
